newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain's mini-Punjab reflects on 50 years history.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain's mini-Punjab reflects on 50 years history.

text.p: The sign outside the local primary school sternly warns against parking in front of the gates -- in English, Hindi, Punjabi and Urdu.
Within shouting distance of the modest building are a mosque, a church, Sikh and Hindu temples, plus the Suman Marriage Bureau, proudly claiming to have arranged 6,000 marriages since 1972.
Just down the road at the corner pub customers can pay in pounds or in rupees as Indian movies blare from several television screens.

This is mini-Punjab, a bustling corner of southwest London named after the border district split between India and Pakistan 50 years ago when Britain granted independence to its former colony and partitioned it into two nations.
Southall is full of residents whose roots go back to the Punjab, some of them Sikhs and Hindus who found themselves on the wrong side of the border and fled the newly-formed Pakistan for India.

Nearly 23,000 ethnic Indians, in addition to more than 3,000 Pakistanis and Bangladeshis, live in the neighbourhood and make up almost 70 percent of its population, according to the latest available data.
Their lives tell the story of India and Britain's intertwined destinies, of penniless immigrants arriving from half a world away and slowly clawing their way to success.
FROM MARKET PEDDLER TO MULTI-MILLIONAIRE
Gurdip Gujral was 13 when his family fled their home in the farming village of Sargodha in Pakistani Punjab in 1947 and moved to India to escape the impending violence.

A decade later, he arrived in England with his young wife and nine-month-old son. Gujral, a burly man with a red turban and the full beard of an orthodox Sikh, took a job as a cleaner in a local factory and moved into a one-room flat in Southall, where he had friends from the Punjab.

Struggling to support his family on a weekly wage of 8.50 pounds ($14.32) a week and aware he would never move up in an English company in the 1960s, Gujral began moonlighting, selling brass trinkets at London's Petticoat Lane market at weekends.

Working his way from market to market across England, Gujral gradually built up an Indian import business -- which last year achieved sales of 12 million pounds. Now a British citizen, he ranks among the wealthiest Asians in the country.

Even after decades in his adopted homeland, Gujral still misses his ancestral home. "We have great friends here. We are British but still we are foreign. There is something missing," he says wistfully.
"I want to go back but my children and grandchildren were born here. They would never leave. This is their home."
But when multi-millionaire broaches the subject of Indian independence, he fills with reproach: "India has achieved nothing in 50 years, only corruption. It has so much potential."
He has equally critical words for his adopted country. "The English have grown very lazy. They have ruled all around the world and have forgotten how to work."
COMMUNIST STUDENT AGITATOR BECOMES A BRITISH MP

Piara Khabra was born into a Sikh farming family in 1924 in Kaharpur, on the Indian side of the Punjab. While at university he became active in the communist youth movement, taking part in student protests throughout India.
"I shared the 'Throw Them Out' nationalist sentiment," admits the balding 72-year-old.

He eventually became a secondary school teacher and then decided to go abroad to continue his studies. After being denied a visa to take up a scholarship in the United States because of his communist links, Khabra made his way to Southall in 1959.
"I was very ambitious, always on the move," he explains.
Like Gujral, his first job was in a factory, at an industrial bakery outside London where he transferred sheets of dough from one production line to another.

No matter how hard he worked he could never have become a factory foreman because of his skin colour, he says. In frustration Khabra took up an office clerical job and, after going to night school, became a qualified teacher.

Building on his student experience he entered the local political fray, at first with no success with the fledgling Communist Party of Great Britain and later as a local Labour Party councillor. The community in Southall rewarded him for his many efforts on its behalf with a seat in the House of Commons, Britain's lower chamber of parliament, in 1992 and again in 1997.

"I look back and wonder how it happened," Khabra says from a dingy office of the Indian Workers' Association, where a growing queue of residents waits silently in the hallway to plead for his assistance.
"I worked so hard for so many years, maybe it was inevitable."
For Khabra the 50th independence anniversary represents a chance to celebrate a remarkable achievement by a group of British subjects.

"We were ruled by a nation thousands of miles away and we overcame the most powerful empire in the world without arms. There was a great joy and happiness at that achievement. It is a very special feeling. I share that."
TRADITIONS NEVER DIE

While Southall's thriving Indian community has become an integral part of London, it has remained distinctly apart, closely retaining its Asian links with little of the "English" feel that has crept into other Indian areas.
The neighbourhood has no official plans for celebrating the August 15 anniversary of Indian independence, perhaps because just walking through its streets is cultural celebration enough.

Corner shops teem with rich fruits, spices and nuts from the subcontinent -- rainbow varieties of split peas, fresh coriander and curry leaves, green and red chillies, dried limes and ground mangoes, even shredded rose petals.
The latest hits in Indian rock music pulse through the streets, while store after store offers highly stylised traditional costumes, pyjamas and reams of patterned sari fabrics.
Tradition remains a focal point of Southall, explains Suman Bhargava, founder and co-owner of the Suman Marriage Bureau.

The Delhi-native, whose Hindu husband hails from the Pakistani part of the Punjab, points to a wall full of photographs of happy couples brought together by her agency. An array of gold bracelets jingles on her arm as she recounts how she has married off entire sets of siblings.

"It is very important to involve the families in these matters because it is not like with the English. With an Asian marriage it is not just the couple who marries but also the two families," she explains.
She opened the matchmaking business in 1972 after friends complained of the difficulties of finding eligible spouses for their children in Britain.

"We provide a valuable service to the Asian community," she says, adding that her files are filled with nearly a thousand eligible men and women. They are carefully broken down by nationality, religion and caste.
"Caste is very important in the overseas community, perhaps even more important than in India. In many respects we are much less modern here."
Bhargava, who also teaches Hindi literature and language, is proud of the role she plays in preserving her community's ties to its traditions and its past.
"Arranged marriages are a link to our history, but they are not outdated. It is the past that makes the future. That is what the 50th anniversary is all about."
($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
